name: Brand expressive
summary: Big display type, vivid color and springy motion, for launches that must be remembered.
description: Brand expressive is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Big display type, vivid color and springy motion, for launches that must be remembered.

ai.use_when: Launch sites, campaigns, marketing pages and consumer brands that lead with personality.
ai.avoid_when: Tools people use for hours, or forms where calm matters more than character.

scenarios.text: A visitor lands on a launch page from a social post and joins the waiting list.
An agency swaps the campaign colors for the next drop without changing the components.

answers.why: Bricolage Grotesque for display and headings, DM Sans for text: loud where the brand speaks, easy where people read.

considers.readability: Body text sits in DM Sans, a low-contrast sans that reads easily in short copy.
considers.legibility: DM Sans keeps simple, open shapes at small sizes; the display face never sets small text.
considers.scalability: Both are variable: Bricolage Grotesque has optical size, width and weight axes, and DM Sans optical size and weight.
considers.numerals: Numbers are few and set in DM Sans, in short copy rather than tables.
considers.scripts: Latin, with accents; other scripts need faces chosen for the same voice.
considers.recognition: Bricolage Grotesque's character is the brand's: people know it by its headlines.
considers.familiarity: DM Sans for text keeps reading familiar while the display face takes the risks.
considers.personality: Bold and confident, as the brand answer asks.
considers.performance: Two variable families, one file each.
considers.licensing: SIL Open Font License, both: free to embed in apps and on the web.
considers.fallback: Falls back to system-ui, as its tokens say; DM Sans is the display face's text pair.

default.label: Brand expressive
default.description: The single brand: vivid magenta, Bricolage Grotesque display, pill controls.

theme.$description: The Brand expressive theme: what each brand-dependent semantic key picks, in light and dark, plus mode-free picks (fonts, corners) in base. Info uses blue, kept apart from the brand color so it never reads as an action. Categories 1 to 5 are pink, blue, green, amber, taupe: distinct hues for tags and chart series, with no meaning. Disabled uses the neutral taupe.

open-ds.why: radius.pill: We use a pill corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a playful tone, by brand convention. A full radius does this by rounding both ends into a capsule, the brand's signature shape. So every action feels bold and friendly, because the brand is bold (brand.q1), controls are pills (shape.values) and each section holds one big idea (content.q2).

radius.pill: We use the pill control corner for badges in order to keep one role family by the badge relation: badges share the control's corner. The same full radius does this by giving a status the capsule of the buttons beside it. So a status pill matches the buttons and the page keeps one shape, because badges get no corner of their own (shape.roles) and controls are pills (shape.values).

radius.20: We use a 20px corner for menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 24px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by following the outer curve at the padding's distance. So an option's curve runs parallel to its menu's curve, because surfaces take 24px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the panel's padding is 4px (spacing.values).

radius.12: We use the 12px box corner for boxes that grow in order to keep them box-shaped objects by the relation: a pill control gives way to the box corner. A moderate radius does this by curving the corners while the sides stay straight as the box grows. So a text area or a list item stays a box, not an oval, because controls are pills (shape.values) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).

radius.24: We use a 24px corner for cards, menus and dialogs in order to make each offer read as a separate object, in a bold tone by brand convention. A large radius does this by breaking the outline with a wide curve while the sides stay straight. shadow.card: We use step 1 of the shadow scale for cards in order to show their height as objects above the page. The cast shade does this by a 12px offset and a 32px blur at 14%. So each offer feels like an object you can pick up, because cards rise too (elevation.roles) and shadows are pronounced (elevation.values).

shadow.overlay: We use step 2 of the shadow scale for menus and dialogs in order to show floating height, one step above the cards. The cast shade does this by a 24px offset and a 48px blur at 20%, larger than the card's. So a menu sits clearly above vivid sections and cards, because cards and overlays rise (elevation.roles) and shadows are pronounced (elevation.values).

The lighter fill does this by the dark-mode depth rule: the higher a layer sits, the lighter its surface. So visitors see a menu above the page even where its shadow barely shows, because dark ships as standard (theming.values) and the roles answer names the layers that rise (elevation.roles).

neutral.floor: We use the floor step, below the page's canvas, for table headers and wells in dark, in order to show depth by tone, 1.13:1 under content and 1.05:1 under the canvas. The darker fill does this by the depth rule turned downward: what sits lower is darker. So a well reads as recessed and never as a raised card, because dark ships as standard (theming.values) and depth reads from tone and lines (elevation.definition).

neutral.floor: We use the floor step, below the canvas, for the item under the pointer or the keyboard in dark, in order to mark it as a band on both surfaces it meets: 1.13:1 on surface.default and 1.37:1 on surface.raised, and 1.05:1 off the page. The fill does this by stepping darker, as raised layers took the lighter step; muted text still reads 7.59:1 on it. So the hovered row or menu item shows on cards and menus alike, because hover and focus have their own look (accessibility.roles) and the neutral ramp sets the steps (color.definition).

neutral.200: We use the step above the raised surface for a pressed item in dark in order to show a press as a change of its own. The fill does this by stepping lighter while the hover band steps darker, 1.91:1 from the highlight, so press and hover never match. So a tap reads under the finger, because pressed has its own look for touch (accessibility.roles) and the neutral ramp sets the steps (color.definition).

shadow.none: We use no shadow for cards in dark in order to keep shadows on floating layers only: menus, popovers, dialogs, toasts and tooltips. The missing shade does this by leaving the card's height to tone: the lighter raised surface and its 1px light ring. So cards still read as lifted on a dark page, without a shade that cannot be seen, because dark ships as standard (theming.values) and cards rise by shadow in light (elevation.roles).

shadow.overlay-dark: We use the light overlay shadow's shape in dark in order to show the same floating height by the dark-shade relation. The cast shade does this by the same 24px offset and 48px blur, at 60% black instead of 20%. So a menu still sits above dark sections, though its shade reads weaker on dark than in light, because cards and overlays rise (elevation.roles) and dark ships as standard (theming.values).

neutral.why: A warm, rosy gray sits under the vivid pink brand without competing.

open-ds.why: Big, even steps give an 8px base. Spacious density opens the layout gaps wide, five and eight steps, so big moments have room.

We use 8px for the tight gap between the parts of one item, such as an icon and its word, in order to group and separate: one base step (1 × 8px), the smallest of the big even steps. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So a call to action reads as one bold unit, because steps are big and even (spacing.definition) and the content is images and campaigns (content.q1).

We use 16px for the default gap between the items of one group in order to group and separate: two base steps (2 × 8px), twice the tight gap. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so air between items keeps big type readable, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and delight is the point (human.q1).

We use 40px for the group gap between groups inside a section in order to group and separate: five base steps (5 × 8px), two and a half default gaps. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so each group has its own moment inside a section, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and each section holds one big idea (content.q2).

We use 64px for the section gap between big sections in order to group and separate: eight base steps (8 × 8px), four default gaps. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so each section, with its color block, is a moment of its own, because space works between big sections (spacing.lands) and the layout is spacious (spacing.values).

We use 28px for the inline padding inside controls in order to give content room inside its box: three and a half base steps (3.5 × 8px), wider than a table cell. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So pill buttons look bold and are easy to hit with a thumb, because the brand is bold (brand.q1) and visitors are on the move (scenarios.q1).

We use 32px for the padding inside cards and dialogs in order to give content room inside its box: four base steps (4 × 8px), twice the default gap. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so each card holds its moment, because delight is the point (human.q1) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).

We use 16px for the inline padding inside table cells in order to give content room inside its box: two base steps (2 × 8px), the same as the default gap. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so the rare table keeps the page's airy rhythm, because the content is images and campaigns, with few tables (content.q1), and the layout is spacious (spacing.values).
A touch target sets the 52px default. Compact is one 8px step below it; large is one step above it, for the one loud sign-up action. The scheme has no row role, so a row takes the default.

default.$description: Height of buttons and inputs, and the smallest target.

open-ds.why: We use 52px for buttons and inputs in order to make a hit target: the touch target size, step 0 of the control scale, a 52px hit area. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So every control fits a thumb, because the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values) and visitors arrive on their phones (scenarios.q1).

We use 44px for compact controls, such as a button inside a pill field, in order to make a hit target: one 8px step below the 52px default on the control scale, a 44px hit area that still fits a thumb. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so a button sits inside the pill field and still fits a thumb, because visitors are on the move (scenarios.q1) and the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values).

large.$description: Height of large controls: the one loud call to action.

open-ds.why: We use 60px for the one loud call to action in order to make a hit target: one 8px step above the 52px default on the control scale, a 60px hit area, as sign-up is the scheme's hero action. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so the sign-up button wins the eye and the thumb, because there is one action, sign up (tasks.q2), and visitors are on the move (scenarios.q1).

We use 52px for one table row in order to keep the eye on its row: by inheritance, as the scheme has no row role and a row holds controls, so size.row takes size.control.default, one 52px control tall. Row height does this by making each row a band the eye follows across, and a hit target when the row is clickable (WCAG 2.5.8: 24px). So the rare table keeps the brand's airy rhythm, because spacing has gaps and insets only (spacing.roles) and the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values).
Icons beside text are 20px, larger than the 17px body, so they hold their own next to big type.

hit-area.$description: The least hit area of a control. A control drawn smaller keeps its size; its hit area grows past it, never into a neighbour.

open-ds.why: We use a 44px hit area for controls drawn smaller, such as a checkbox, a radio or a switch, in order to make a hit target a fingertip can find: the WCAG 2.5.5 size. The hit area does this by growing past the drawn box through a pseudo-element, and rows in a group stand at least 44px apart, so no two targets overlap. So visitors tap the right control on a phone, because targets are sized for touch (accessibility.values) and the layout leaves room for it (spacing.values).

badge.$description: Corner of badges, chips, tooltips, keyboard keys (kbd) and checkboxes: small labels and marks.

option.$description: Corner of options in menus and lists: the panel's corner less its padding, so the corners nest.

element.$description: Corner of an element that holds content and can grow past one line: a list item, an accordion row, a text area, a calendar, an attachment, a skeleton or media.

surface.$description: Corner of cards, menus and dialogs.

open-ds.why: We use a 2px default line for card borders in order to give grouping in a bold tone. A heavier stroke does this by drawing a shared region with the weight of the bold type beside it. So each card holds its offer next to vivid color, because cards separate groups (elevation.definition), AA holds on every color (accessibility.definition) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).

width.$description: The focus ring's width: one step heavier than the default border, and not a border width.

open-ds.why: We use a 3px focus ring in order to show focus, one step heavier than the 2px default line by the focus relation. A heavier stroke does this by standing out even from the bold edges around it. So keyboard users see focus on vivid color, because focus has its own look (accessibility.roles) and AA holds on every color (accessibility.definition).

offset.$description: The gap between a control and its focus ring, so the ring never touches the control and reads on any fill.

open-ds.why: We use a fixed 2px focus offset in order to keep focus visible by contrast, not for style. The gap does this by showing the page color between ring and control, so one of the two colors keeps enough contrast against any fill (W3C technique C40). So visitors see the ring on any brand color, because focus has its own look (accessibility.roles).
Many fine steps: a regular 17px body and a 1.114 ratio, with wide gaps up to the display, so big moments have room. Headlines and labels sit tight at 1.1; text that wraps opens to 1.55.
Display sets 56px, eleven fine steps above the 17px body (17 × 1.114^11), the top of the scale, because every hero opens with one big idea in the brand's loudest voice.
Display lines use 1.1, the tight ratio the scheme gives its big sizes, so a 56px headline stacks as one bold block.
Display sets weight 800, the heaviest step, because the hero headline carries the bold, loud brand.
Title sets 40px, eight steps above body and three under display, so the sign-up form's title stays big and keeps the form in view on a phone.
Title lines use 1.1 like display, because a 40px title is still a headline size in the proportional scale.
Title keeps weight 800 from display, so the form page still speaks in the brand's bold headline voice.

Heading sets 28px, five steps above body (17 × 1.114^5 = 29.2) snapped to the 4px grid, and three under the 40px title, the smallest headline step, so it carries the display face into cards and dialogs.
Heading lines use 1.1, the headline ratio, because headings stay short: three to six words, as the voice asks.
Heading drops to weight 700, one step under display and title, so cards stay bold without shouting over the hero.
Body sets 17px in DM Sans, step 0 of the scale, so short punchy copy reads easily on the phones visitors arrive on.
Body lines open to 1.55, the relaxed ratio, so DM Sans copy reads easily while display lines sit tight at 1.1.
Body stays at weight 400, regular, because the display does the shouting and the text only has to read.
Label sets 15px, one step under body and one over the 14px caption, so field labels stay readable on vivid color.
Labels use the tight 1.1 ratio, because a label is one short line beside a pill control.
Labels set weight 700, bold DM Sans, so a field label holds on vivid color and matches the bold brand.
Caption sets 14px, two steps under the 17px body, the smallest step, so fine print stays small and headlines keep the attention that wins sign-ups.
Captions keep the 1.55 body ratio, so small fine print in DM Sans stays easy to read across lines.
Captions stay at weight 400, regular, so fine print never pulls the eye from the bold headlines.
Data shares step 0 with body at 17px, because tables are rare and short, so cells read like the rest of the page.
Data cells keep the body's 1.55 ratio, so a rare table keeps the page's airy rhythm.
Data stays at weight 400, regular DM Sans, so numbers in short copy keep the brand's text voice.

feedback.$description: Hover, press and toggle feedback. At most 500ms in an expressive family.

open-ds.why: We use 120ms (fast) for hover, press and toggle feedback in order to answer each tap at once, well inside the expressive limit of 500ms. The duration does this by ending the change before the finger lifts. So visitors feel the brand respond, never lag, because motion carries expression (motion.roles) and feedback feels fast (motion.values).

panels.$description: Menus, popovers, dialogs and drawers opening. At most 500ms in an expressive family.

open-ds.why: We use 200ms (moderate) for menus, popovers, dialogs and other panels in order to show where a panel comes from, inside the expressive limit of 500ms. The duration does this by giving the eye time to follow the panel from its trigger. So visitors see each menu arrive as part of the brand, because the family is expressive (motion.roles) and there are three speeds (motion.count).

exit.$description: A layer closing: shorter than its open.

open-ds.why: We use the feedback duration, 120ms (fast), for a layer that closes in order to end the exit move faster than the 200ms open. The duration does this by removing what people are done with in fewer frames than it took to arrive. So visitors get back to the page at once, because even an expressive family keeps exits short (motion.roles) and there are three speeds (motion.count).

hero.$description: Hero and launch moments. At most 500ms in an expressive family.

open-ds.why: We use 320ms (relaxed) for hero and launch moments in order to give the slowest move to the moment that matters most, inside the expressive limit of 500ms. The duration does this by holding the change long enough to be seen as an event. So every visitor sees the launch, because motion shows in hero moments (motion.lands) and the family is expressive (motion.roles).

standard.$description: The transition move: a state that changes in place, such as hover, press or toggle.

open-ds.why: We use the standard easing (0.2, 0, 0, 1) for state changes in place in order to do the transition move without the spring. The curve does this by reaching its target early and settling, with no overshoot. So buttons and toggles feel quick and steady, and the bounce stays special, because the spring is for emphasis only (motion.definition) in an expressive family (motion.roles).

enter.$description: The enter move: a layer that appears.

open-ds.why: We use the transition move's standard easing for a panel that appears in order to do the enter move. The curve does this by spending most of the change in the first frames, so the layer is in place before it slows. So a menu is readable almost as soon as it opens, because an expressive family keeps its spring for emphasis (motion.roles) and enters on an ease-out (motion.definition).

exit.$description: The exit move: a layer that closes in place.

open-ds.why: We use the strong-out easing (0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) for a layer that closes in place in order to do the exit move. The curve does this by covering most of the way in the first third of its time, then easing to a stop. So a closed popover is gone before the next tap, because an expressive exit eases out unless the layer leaves the screen (motion.roles), and easing is set per move (motion.definition).

exit-offscreen.$description: The exit move of a layer that slides off the screen: a sheet or a drawer.

open-ds.why: We use the accelerate easing (0.4, 0, 1, 1) for a drawer or sheet that slides off the screen in order to do the exit move of a layer that leaves the view. The curve does this by starting slow and speeding up, so the panel gathers pace on its way out. So visitors read the drawer as gone, not paused at the edge, because an expressive family accelerates only what leaves the screen (motion.roles) and easing is set per move (motion.definition).

emphasize.$description: The emphasize move: a moment that calls for attention. The only move that overshoots.

open-ds.why: We use the spring easing (0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1) for the emphasize move only, in order to celebrate a moment such as a sign-up that worked. The curve does this by passing its target and settling back, so the eye catches the bounce. So the brand's spring is felt where it means something, not on every menu, because easing is a spring (motion.definition) and motion carries expression (motion.roles).

neutral.$description: The neutral scale: the scheme's gray, step by step. Surfaces, borders and text read it, never a gray directly.

highlight.$description: The item the pointer or the keyboard is on.

pressed.$description: The item while it is pressed.

scrim.$description: Dims the page behind a dialog.

on-light.$description: Text on any light fill, in either mode.

on-dark.$description: Text on any dark fill, in either mode.

info-on-light.$description: Info text on a light info fill, such as its tint in light mode.

info-on-dark.$description: Info text on a dark info fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

success-on-light.$description: Success text on a light success fill, such as its tint in light mode.

success-on-dark.$description: Success text on a dark success fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

warning-on-light.$description: Warning text on a light warning fill, such as its tint in light mode.

warning-on-dark.$description: Warning text on a dark warning fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

danger-on-light.$description: Danger text on a light danger fill, such as its tint in light mode.

danger-on-dark.$description: Danger text on a dark danger fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

raised.$description: The 1px edge of a raised layer: menus, dialogs and toasts, and raised cards.

selected.$description: The edge that marks a selected item, so selection is never color alone.

@.$description: The fill of a destructive commit: the confirm of a delete.
Info text and icons: neutral news, no action needed.
Category 1: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 2: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 3: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 4: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 5: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.

category.$description: Colors with no meaning, for content that needs telling apart: decorative accents and non-semantic blocks such as tags, labels and chart series.

disabled.$description: The shared look of controls that cannot be used right now.

text.$description: Text and icons of a disabled control.

open-ds.why: Spacious: big space makes big moments, so panels double their room; rows stay tight.

stroke-width.$description: The line weight of every icon, on Lucide's 24px grid.

open-ds.why: Icons use a 1.75 stroke width on Lucide's 24px grid, a firm line that carries the brand's bold warmth.

background.$description: Card fill: a raised layer, lighter than content in dark.

border.$description: Card edge: the raised ring, a solid lighter step in dark.

focus-ring-invalid.$description: Chips focus ring invalid of the combobox.
Focus ring invalid of the input group.
Slot focus ring invalid of the input otp.
Focus ring invalid of the native select.

radius.$description: Item radius of the radio group.
Group label radius of the sidebar.
Menu badge radius of the sidebar.
Menu skeleton radius of the sidebar.
Menu sub button radius of the sidebar.
Corner of the menu button, of the sidebar.
Corner of the switch's thumb: round, as the track is.

focus-ring-invalid.$description: Focus ring invalid of the textarea.

size-large.$description: Size of the large icon, where the scheme has two sizes.

content.$description: Voice tokens: the words components use for common actions. Text, not CSS.

commit.$description: The label of the action that completes a task.

cancel.$description: The label of the way out next to the main action.

destroy.$description: The label of an action that deletes data.

retry.$description: The label that repeats a failed action.

empty-action.$description: The label of the action in an empty state.
